solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Places one can get on with boob jobs, I'm told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the words are judged by sound

parts.note: breast operations, i.e. bust ops, said quickly

explanation.surface: A cheeky remark about cosmetic surgery clinics as places to get ahead in life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on' sounds like progress in life, but here it means boarding a bus.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus stop is a roadside point where passengers board public transport.

clue.text: Might one buzz in during summer competition

definitions.text: Might one buzz in during summer
definitions.meaning: first meaning: an insect humming about in the warm months

explanation.surface: A quiz contestant wondering whether to hit the buzzer in a summer contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buzz in' suggests a quiz buzzer; the competition is a separate meaning, a spelling bee.
explanation.definitionFit: The insect hums through summer, and a bee is also a gathering for a contest such as spelling.

clue.text: Religious college? Cut class!

indicators.note: cutting a word trims something off it, here its final letter

explanation.surface: A student at a religious college deciding to skip a lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut class' reads as playing truant; Cut instead docks the last letter of the college, and class is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A seminar is a small teaching session where a group discusses a topic with a tutor.

clue.text: Rubbish journey, ending in trouble

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is kept

explanation.surface: A dreadful journey that ended badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is informal for nonsense or worthless stuff, from the cheap offal.

clue.text: 17 perhaps tucking in to finish up French soups

indicators.note: something tucked in is placed inside another word
in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: seventeen is an example of an age; the clue number here is read as the number itself

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper tucking into French soups to finish off a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 looks like a cross-reference to KEEPER, but the number simply stands for an age. POTS takes AGE inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Potage is French for a thick soup, so the plural names several such soups.

clue.text: Pop over to visit son and pop

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside another place, so one piece sits within the others

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for over
pop and da are both informal names for father

explanation.surface: Dad dropping by to see his son.
explanation.walkthrough: The first Pop is the fizzy drink; the second is father. O goes between S and DA.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda and pop are both everyday names for a fizzy soft drink.

clue.text: Some about rodeo did this to those they beat

definitions.text: did this to those they beat

indicators.note: some of the letters means only part of the following words is used

parts.note: the letters run from inside about into rodeo

explanation.surface: Some riders at a rodeo got the better of those they beat.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole later phrase: riders who win at a rodeo ride faster than those beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: To outride someone is to ride better or faster than them, so winners did that to losers.

clue.text: A typical cop raging like there's no tomorrow!

indicators.note: something raging is wild and out of control, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: An ordinary police officer flying into a wild rage.
explanation.definitionFit: Apocalyptic describes the end of the world, a time after which there is no next day.

clue.text: Band name that's confused A&R

indicators.note: confusing two letters means mistaking one for the other, so one letter is swapped for its partner

parts.note: a term is a name for something

explanation.surface: A band named by record-company A&R staff who mixed things up.
explanation.walkthrough: A&R is the music-industry artists-and-repertoire department, apt for a band; here it means the letters A and R. Swap TERM's R for A.
explanation.definitionFit: A band is a group working together, which is what a team is.

clue.text: The way one pitches things at home to people

parts.note: to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: How a salesperson pitches products to people at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitches' suggests a sales pitch; here it is the pitch of the voice.
explanation.definitionFit: Intonation is the rise and fall in vocal pitch while speaking.

clue.text: Celebrity performing with a turn on board

indicators.note: given a turn, a word is spun around to face the other way

parts.note: a show that is on is being performed
board in the old sense of a table for meals

explanation.surface: A star performing a pirouette on a stage board.
explanation.definitionFit: A notable is a noun for a well-known or important person.

clue.text: Detective leaving gap in policy

indicators.note: something leaving is taken out, so these letters are removed from the word

parts.note: a gap or space between things

explanation.surface: A detective spotting a loophole in procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gap in policy' reads as a loophole, but in is a link, policy the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A stance is a stated position or attitude on an issue, close to a policy.

clue.text: Hoisted film cast up a tree with Mr T

indicators.note: in a down entry, hoisting lifts a word so it reads upward
to cast is to throw, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, joining the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A film crew stuck up a tree with the A-Team actor Mr T.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr T looks like one name, but the T alone is the definition: T is the scientific symbol for temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: In physics formulas the letter T is the standard symbol for temperature.

clue.text: Miss turn-off, but carry on regardless?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: drive past the exit you wanted
second meaning: push on beyond acceptable limits

explanation.walkthrough: The literal driving sense and the figurative sense of overstepping the mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Overshooting a junction means travelling past it, and overstepping limits is the idiom's figurative sense.

clue.text: Beer scam drunk takes to heart

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so these letters lurch into a new order

explanation.surface: A drunkard who falls for a dodgy beer deal.
explanation.definitionFit: To embrace an idea is to adopt it wholeheartedly, as is taking it to heart.

clue.text: Motor I purchased with 50% off is a beast

indicators.note: taking 50% off means losing half the word's letters

explanation.surface: A car bought at half price that turns out to be a monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beast' sounds like an insult to the car; it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The caribou is the North American reindeer, a large wild animal.

clue.text: Extras in Cheers

wordplay.note: a bye is a cricket extra, a run scored without the bat; two of them make extras

explanation.surface: Film extras appearing in the sitcom Cheers.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheers is the US sitcom in the surface, but in Britain cheers is also an everyday way of saying goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheers is informal British for goodbye or thanks, and bye-bye is a casual farewell.

clue.text: Perhaps one's intended caretaker

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a partner worth holding on to
second meaning: a custodian who looks after something

explanation.walkthrough: A fiancé may well be a keeper in the slang sense of someone worth not letting go.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang calls a partner worth marrying a keeper, and a custodian of a place or animals is likewise one.

clue.text: Arrogant English cat (according to vocal Aussie)

parts.note: Pom is Australian slang for an English person

indicators.note: this is how the words would come out when spoken in an Australian accent

parts.note: puss, as an Australian voice might stretch the vowel

explanation.surface: An Australian's jibe at a stuck-up English cat.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitting that an Aussie supplies Pom, the Australian slang for a Brit.
explanation.definitionFit: Pompous means self-important and full of airs, close to arrogant.

clue.text: Cold English wife splits, stealing heart of Harry Styles

indicators.note: a thief takes something and holds it, so one piece is placed inside another
the heart of a word is its central part, so only middle letters are kept

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Gossip that a wife is leaving her husband for pop star Harry Styles.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Styles is a pop singer, but Styles alone is the definition, hairstyles. CEW takes R inside before CUTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A crew cut is a very short hairstyle, so crew cuts are styles of haircut.

clue.text: Make loads of bread and put it all away

definitions.meaning: first meaning: earn a great deal of money, bread being slang for money
second meaning: tidy everything back into place

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a baker's day: bake, then tidy. Bread is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: To clean up is idiom for making big profits, and literally means tidying things away.

clue.text: Pardon prisoner number 24

parts.note: 24 across is OVER, and over means finished, done

explanation.surface: A prisoner, number 24, given a pardon.
explanation.walkthrough: Number 24 reads as a prison number; it points to the answer at 24 across.
explanation.definitionFit: To condone is to overlook or forgive an offence, much as a pardon excuses it.

clue.text: Story about member fit to raise Cain?

indicators.note: one word goes around the other, enclosing it

parts.note: an arm is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: A tale about a body part that could cause an uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise Cain' means make trouble, but Cain in Genesis was a tiller of the soil; land fit to raise his crops is farmable.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmable land can be cultivated, and Cain was a farmer, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Very pleasant touring eastern city

indicators.note: touring means going around, so one word wraps around a letter

explanation.surface: A traveller finds touring an eastern city very pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Venice is the Italian city built on canals.

clue.text: Very Russian girl — one with a big mouth?

explanation.surface: A very loud Russian girl who talks too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big mouth' suggests a chatterbox; a river has a mouth, and the Volga is Europe's longest river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Volga is a vast Russian river with a wide delta where it meets the Caspian Sea.

clue.text: The French Connection?

parts.note: surface reading: the 1971 drug-smuggling film, or a fashion brand
setter's reading: the physical link joining Britain to France under the sea

explanation.walkthrough: The title evokes the film; read literally it is whatever connects England to France.
explanation.definitionFit: The rail tunnel under the Channel is the literal link between Britain and France.

clue.text: Bit of opinion vicar rejected as "load of balls!"

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small piece of it, here its first letter
something rejected is sent back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: Rev is short for Reverend, a vicar's title

explanation.surface: A vicar's view dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Load of balls' sounds like an insult; in cricket an over is a set of six balls.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket an over is a batch of six deliveries bowled by one bowler.

clue.text: Consume with worry

explanation.walkthrough: 'Consumed with worry' is a phrase; split it into two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Eat means to swallow food, and also to bother someone, as in asking what is eating them.

clue.text: Direction one could take being bust post-Brexit?

indicators.note: Brexit is Britain's exit, so after it the letters standing for Britain have gone

explanation.surface: Which way the country might head with the economy broke after leaving the EU.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' reads as broke; it is the chest. BR is the abbreviation for Britain, which exits the word.
explanation.definitionFit: East is one of the four compass points, a direction someone may head.

clue.text: Superficial secretary upset Young Ones producer

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the word is turned back to front

parts.note: a PA is a personal assistant

explanation.surface: A shallow secretary annoying the producer of the sitcom The Young Ones.
explanation.walkthrough: The Young Ones was a 1980s British TV comedy; here young ones are offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparent means seeming so on the surface, which is what superficial describes.
